skill.name: defi-protocol-templates
skill.description: Draft and review educational Solidity templates for staking, automated market makers, governance, and flash loans.
skill.summary: Use DeFi contract examples as starting points for design, testing, and security review.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: All 26 static findings are false positives caused by Solidity require statements and Markdown backticks, not dynamic loading, command execution, or reconnaissance. Semantic review found exploitable token-handling and receiver-authorization flaws, missing slippage protections, and a broken flash-loan repayment flow in examples described as production-ready.

remediation.issue: The flash-loan receiver approves any caller for an arbitrary token amount.
remediation.suggestion: Store the trusted provider, require callbacks from that address, validate the asset, and limit approvals to the exact repayment.

remediation.issue: Contracts ignore ERC20 transfer return values and assume requested amounts equal received amounts.
remediation.suggestion: Use SafeERC20 and derive accounting from balance changes, or explicitly reject unsupported fee-on-transfer and rebasing tokens.

remediation.issue: AMM entry points provide no minimum-output, minimum-share, or deadline parameters.
remediation.suggestion: Add user-defined slippage bounds and deadlines, then test sandwich, stale-transaction, and fee-on-transfer scenarios.

remediation.issue: The sample receiver approves repayment, but the provider never collects the approved amount.
remediation.suggestion: Define one repayment model and implement it consistently. Pull repayment with SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom or require a direct transfer before returning.

remediation.issue: The skill labels unaudited examples as production-ready.
remediation.suggestion: Describe them as educational starting points and add explicit test, dependency-version, threat-model, and audit requirements.

semantic_findings.title: Unauthenticated Flash-Loan Callback Grants Token Allowance
semantic_findings.description: The receiver accepts calls from any address and approves that caller to spend the requested asset. An attacker can request an allowance and drain held tokens.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The callback has no caller or asset validation and directly approves msg.sender for amount plus fee. This creates a clear unauthorized-spending path.

semantic_findings.title: Unsafe ERC20 Transfer and Accounting Assumptions
semantic_findings.description: Several contracts ignore ERC20 return values and update accounting from requested amounts. Failed or fee-charging transfers can create unbacked balances, shares, or payouts.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The examples call transfer and transferFrom without SafeERC20 or return checks, while state changes use nominal inputs. Nonstandard ERC20 behavior makes the accounting unsafe.

semantic_findings.title: AMM Omits User Slippage and Deadline Controls
semantic_findings.description: Liquidity and swap functions accept no minimum return or deadline. Users cannot constrain adverse price movement, enabling sandwich losses and stale execution.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The public AMM methods expose only amounts and token selection. No minimum shares, minimum output, maximum input, or transaction deadline is enforced.

semantic_findings.title: Flash-Loan Repayment Flow Is Inconsistent
semantic_findings.description: The receiver grants an allowance, but the provider never pulls repayment. The sample receiver therefore leaves the provider balance unchanged and positive-fee loans revert.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The provider only checks its final balance, while the receiver only calls approve. No transferFrom or direct repayment connects those operations.

semantic_findings.title: Unaudited Examples Are Presented as Production-Ready
semantic_findings.description: The skill calls these templates production-ready despite exploitable authorization and token-accounting flaws. This claim may encourage unsafe deployment without required hardening.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The production-ready claim is explicit, while the document itself recommends testing and professional audits and contains concrete exploitable flaws.

content.value_statement: DeFi contracts are difficult to design and secure. This skill provides Solidity starting points for staking, AMMs, governance, and flash loans, with validation guidance.
actual_capabilities: Draft staking reward accounting with ERC20 token interfaces.
Outline constant-product AMM liquidity and swap calculations.
Create a governance token and basic proposal voting flow.
Illustrate flash-loan provider and receiver callback structures.
Recommend testing, monitoring, audits, timelocks, multisignature controls, and emergency stops.
limitations: The examples are educational starting points, not audited production contracts.
No lending contract is included despite lending references in the stated scope.
OpenZeppelin imports and overrides may require changes for the selected dependency version.
Templates omit important token compatibility, slippage, authorization, oracle, and governance protections.

use_cases.title: Prototype a DeFi Contract
use_cases.description: Adapt a staking or AMM example into an initial design for local testing.

use_cases.title: Compare Protocol Components
use_cases.description: Review reward, liquidity, voting, and callback patterns before selecting an architecture.

use_cases.title: Plan a Security Review
use_cases.description: Identify missing controls and create a hardening checklist before implementation.

prompt_templates.title: Choose a Template
prompt_templates.prompt: Explain which included template best fits [protocol idea]. List required inputs, key assumptions, and the first tests to write.
prompt_templates.scenario: A beginner needs to select a suitable protocol pattern.

prompt_templates.title: Adapt a Staking Design
prompt_templates.prompt: Adapt the staking example for [staking token] and [reward token]. Define reward funding, duration, withdrawal rules, and test cases without claiming production readiness.
prompt_templates.scenario: A developer needs a concrete staking prototype specification.

prompt_templates.title: Review an AMM
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the AMM template for slippage, token compatibility, reserve accounting, reentrancy, and economic attacks. Return prioritized changes and verification steps.
prompt_templates.scenario: A protocol team is evaluating an AMM starting point.

prompt_templates.title: Create a DeFi Threat Model
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a threat model for [protocol design]. Cover trust boundaries, privileged roles, oracle risks, governance capture, token behavior, invariants, and incident controls.
prompt_templates.scenario: An advanced team needs a security plan before implementation.

output_examples.input: Compare the staking and AMM examples for a rewards platform.
output: Use staking when users deposit one asset to earn funded rewards.
Use an AMM when users supply paired assets and traders need swaps.
Define funding, withdrawal, token behavior, and emergency controls before implementation.

output_examples.input: Review the flash-loan example before local testing.
output: Restrict callbacks to the trusted provider and validate the asset.
Choose direct repayment or provider-initiated transfer and implement one complete flow.
Test unauthorized callbacks, failed transfers, fee rounding, reentrancy, and insufficient repayment.

output_examples.input: Prepare the AMM template for a security review.
output_examples.output: Add slippage limits and deadlines, use safe token transfers, document supported tokens, define invariants, and test adversarial transaction ordering.

best_practices: Treat every template as a starting point and require independent security review before deployment.
Add safe token transfers, explicit access control, slippage limits, timelocks, and emergency controls where appropriate.
Test standard, fee-charging, rebasing, callback-enabled, and malicious token behavior against documented invariants.
anti_patterns: Deploy the examples unchanged or describe them as audited contracts.
Assume every ERC20 transfer succeeds or delivers the requested amount.
Add protocol features before defining trust boundaries, economic invariants, and failure recovery.

faq.question: Are these contracts ready for mainnet?
faq.answer: No. They require dependency updates, protocol-specific design, extensive testing, economic analysis, and an independent security audit.

faq.question: Which protocol examples are included?
faq.answer: The skill includes staking, AMM, governance token, basic governor, flash-loan provider, and receiver examples.

faq.question: Does the skill include a lending implementation?
faq.answer: No. Lending appears in the stated scope and resource list, but no lending contract is present in this file.

faq.question: Which OpenZeppelin version should I use?
faq.answer: Select a supported version first, then update imports, constructors, hooks, and overrides to match its documentation.

faq.question: Can the skill perform a professional audit?
faq.answer: No. It can support review planning and identify common gaps, but it cannot replace independent expert assessment.

faq.question: What should I test first?
faq.answer: Start with authorization, accounting invariants, token transfer failures, reentrancy, rounding, slippage, governance boundaries, and emergency behavior.
